why: A static site on Amazon S3 plus AWS Lambda for resizing is fully serverless: S3 is highly available across multiple AZs and Lambda scales automatically per upload, which handles unpredictable traffic and maximizes scalability. Resized images are stored back in S3, which is cheap and durable for object storage.

others.B: CloudFront does not host or execute a website by itself and storing images in Amazon RDS is a poor fit for binary objects.
others.C: A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure and does not scale automatically with unpredictable traffic.
others.D: Processing resize jobs on a single EC2 instance limits scalability and adds operational overhead compared with Lambda.

tip: Image upload plus transform with unpredictable traffic: S3 event notification to Lambda, results back to S3.

why: With a private-only EKS API endpoint and nodes in private subnets without internet access, nodes must reach AWS services such as Amazon ECR, Amazon EC2, Amazon S3 and AWS STS privately. Creating interface VPC endpoints (plus the S3 gateway endpoint) lets the nodes pull images and register with the cluster without leaving the VPC.

others.A: The node IAM role permissions are standard managed policies; the issue here is network reachability to required AWS service endpoints, not IAM.
others.C: Moving nodes to public subnets violates the compliance requirement that the data plane stays private.
others.D: Security groups allow all outbound by default; without a route or endpoint to AWS services, opening egress rules alone does not help.

tip: Private EKS cluster without NAT: add VPC endpoints for ECR (api and dkr), S3, EC2, STS and CloudWatch Logs.

why: Amazon Redshift supports encryption at rest with AWS KMS or HSM and client-side encryption of loaded data (B), it is built for analytics and BI workloads that can run on a schedule or with pause/resume when the app is idle (C), and it scales to petabytes of data with concurrency scaling and RA3 managed storage (E).

others.A: Serving low-latency data APIs to transactional, containerized and event-driven applications is an OLTP pattern better met by DynamoDB or Aurora, not a data warehouse.
others.D: Caching to offload a backend database is the job of ElastiCache or DAX, not Redshift.
others.F: Redshift has no console feature to create a secondary read replica of a cluster; resilience comes from snapshots, cross-Region snapshot copy and Multi-AZ.

tip: Redshift = OLAP data warehouse; caching = ElastiCache; replicas are an RDS/Aurora concept.

why: API Gateway with AWS Lambda is serverless, so there is no cluster or host to manage, giving the least operational overhead. Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of execution environments pre-initialized, eliminating cold starts so latency stays consistently low during peak periods.

others.A: ALB with ECS requires managing tasks, capacity and scaling policies, which is more overhead than Lambda.
others.C: An EKS cluster adds significant operational overhead for Kubernetes management.
others.D: Reserved concurrency only caps or guarantees a share of concurrency; it does not pre-warm environments, so cold starts can still add latency.

tip: Provisioned concurrency = no cold starts; reserved concurrency = concurrency limit/guarantee.

why: Session Manager has built-in session logging: in the Session Manager preferences you can enable S3 logging and choose a bucket (optionally encrypted), and session data is uploaded automatically. This needs no agents, pipelines or scheduled jobs, so it is the most operationally efficient.

others.B: Installing the CloudWatch agent and exporting log groups to S3 is manual and adds steps; exports are not continuous.
others.C: A custom SSM document run daily by EventBridge is extra custom work and does not capture session data specifically.
others.D: CloudWatch agent plus subscription filter plus Firehose works but is much more infrastructure than the native S3 logging option.

why: RDS storage autoscaling automatically increases allocated storage when free space runs low, with no downtime and no ongoing manual effort once enabled. This directly solves the low disk space problem with the least effort.

others.B: Changing the instance class changes CPU and memory, not storage, and usually causes a brief outage.
others.C: Switching to Provisioned IOPS changes performance characteristics, not capacity, and does not address running out of space.
others.D: Backup, restore and cutover involves downtime and far more effort.

tip: RDS low on storage with no downtime: enable storage autoscaling with a maximum storage threshold.

why: AWS Service Catalog lets an organization centrally create, manage and distribute approved portfolios of products (backed by CloudFormation templates) that end users can launch on a self-service basis with governance controls. That matches centrally managing and deploying a common set of solutions for customer self-service.

others.A: Raw CloudFormation templates can be shared but provide no central catalog, versioning governance or self-service portal.
others.C: Systems Manager documents automate operational tasks on instances, not distribution of solution products.
others.D: AWS Config items record resource configuration state; they do not deploy solutions.

tip: Self-service, centrally approved products = AWS Service Catalog.

why: On-demand capacity mode scales instantly with unpredictable traffic and you pay only per request, avoiding over-provisioning or throttling during spikes. The Standard table class is the cost-effective choice when throughput is moderate to high, since Standard-IA lowers storage cost but raises per-request cost.

others.A: Provisioned with auto scaling reacts slowly to sudden spikes and suits predictable traffic; unpredictable traffic favors on-demand.
others.C: Standard-IA is meant for storage-heavy, rarely accessed tables; with moderate to high throughput it costs more, and provisioned mode fits unpredictable traffic poorly.
others.D: Standard-IA has higher read and write request pricing, which is more expensive for a moderate to high throughput workload.

tip: Unpredictable traffic = on-demand; Standard-IA only when storage dominates cost.

why: Cross-account IAM roles with STS AssumeRole give the application temporary, automatically expiring credentials and least-privilege access defined per business account. The trust policy restricts which role in the inventory account can assume BU_ROLE, so no long-term secrets are stored or rotated.

others.A: DynamoDB does not use database credentials stored in Secrets Manager; access is through IAM, so storing keys as secrets is less secure than temporary role credentials.
others.B: DynamoDB does not support certificate-based authentication for API access.
others.D: ACM certificates are for TLS, not for authenticating callers to DynamoDB.

tip: Cross-account access to AWS APIs: IAM role with trust policy plus sts:AssumeRole.

why: The Kubernetes Metrics Server supplies CPU and memory metrics so the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can add or remove pods based on load, and the Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes worker nodes when pods are unschedulable or nodes are underused. Together they scale both pods and nodes with standard, low-overhead tooling.

others.A: A custom Lambda to resize the cluster is bespoke code that adds operational overhead.
others.D: API Gateway is for exposing APIs and does not scale EKS capacity.
others.E: App Mesh provides service mesh observability and traffic control, not autoscaling.

tip: EKS scaling: HPA (with Metrics Server) for pods, Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter for nodes.

why: AWS AppSync pipeline resolvers execute an ordered sequence of functions that can read from multiple DynamoDB tables in a single GraphQL request, as a fully managed serverless service. The data retrieval is handled by AppSync rather than the application code, so baseline application performance is not affected and operational effort is minimal.

others.B: Lambda@Edge is for customizing CloudFront requests and responses at the edge, not for aggregating data from multiple DynamoDB tables.
others.C: API Gateway with Lambda works but requires writing and maintaining custom aggregation code; edge-optimized endpoints do not help data retrieval.
others.D: Athena Federated Query is for ad hoc analytic SQL and has seconds-level latency, unsuitable for application requests.

tip: Combine multiple data sources in one API call serverlessly: AppSync (GraphQL) resolvers.

why: Amazon Athena can query CloudTrail logs in S3 directly with SQL (the CloudTrail console can even create the Athena table), so you can filter on errorCode values such as AccessDenied and UnauthorizedOperation without building anything. It is serverless and needs only queries, giving the least effort.

others.A: Writing AWS Glue custom scripts is more development effort than SQL queries in Athena.
others.B: AWS Batch with custom scripts requires building and managing compute jobs, which is far more effort.
others.D: QuickSight is a visualization tool and would still need a query layer such as Athena; building dashboards is extra effort.

tip: Ad hoc SQL over logs in S3 (CloudTrail, ALB, VPC Flow Logs) = Athena.

why: The AWS Cost Explorer API provides programmatic access to historical cost and usage data (GetCostAndUsage) and forecasts up to 12 months ahead (GetCostForecast), with pagination for large result sets. It can feed a dashboard directly with no extra infrastructure, so it has the least operational overhead.

others.B: Downloading CSV reports is manual and not programmatic.
others.C: AWS Budgets actions apply controls such as IAM or SCP policies when thresholds are reached; they do not send cost data over FTP.
others.D: Budgets reports are emailed summaries, not programmatic access, and they do not provide full 12-month forecasts for a dashboard.

tip: Programmatic cost data and forecasts = Cost Explorer API.

why: Amazon RDS Proxy keeps a pool of database connections and, during an Aurora failover, routes to the new writer without relying on DNS propagation, cutting failover time by up to 66 percent. The application only needs to switch to the proxy endpoint, so it is the lowest-overhead way to reduce downtime.

others.A: More read replicas give more failover targets but do not reduce the DNS and connection reestablishment delay that causes the downtime.
others.B: A second cluster with manual endpoint switching adds cost, replication complexity and more downtime risk.
others.C: An ElastiCache cache can serve some reads but cannot accept writes during the writer failover and adds caching logic.

tip: Faster failover and connection pooling for RDS or Aurora = RDS Proxy.

why: Deploying the web and application tiers in a second Region, using an Aurora global database with storage-level replication (typically under 1 second lag) to that Region, and Route 53 failover routing gives full Regional redundancy. If the primary Region fails, the secondary cluster is promoted to primary, providing the most fault tolerance.

others.A: An Auto Scaling group is a Regional construct and cannot span Availability Zones in a second Region.
others.B: Aurora PostgreSQL does not support standalone cross-Region read replicas; cross-Region replication for it is through Aurora global database.
others.C: AWS DMS replication adds lag and operational overhead and is less resilient than native Aurora global database replication.

tip: Multi-Region Aurora with fast recovery = Aurora Global Database plus Route 53 failover.

why: AWS Transfer Family provides a managed FTP endpoint that writes directly to Amazon S3, so FTP clients need minimal changes and there is no server to run. An S3 event notification invokes Lambda per file as soon as it arrives, and each 3-8 minute job fits within Lambda's 15-minute limit; the function deletes the object when done, making this the most operationally efficient.

others.A: A self-managed EC2 FTP server and nightly processing from Glacier Flexible Retrieval (which needs restores) defeats the goal of processing files as soon as possible.
others.B: A self-managed FTP server on EC2 with nightly batch processing keeps the delay and adds operational overhead.
others.C: Transfer Family stores files in S3 or EFS, not EBS, and S3 event notifications cannot fire for files on an EBS volume.

tip: Managed SFTP/FTP/FTPS into S3 = AWS Transfer Family; per-file processing under 15 minutes = S3 event to Lambda.

why: Amazon RDS is a managed database service that handles patching, backups and high availability, reducing operational overhead for transactional databases. Enabling encryption at rest with AWS KMS protects the sensitive data in storage, backups, snapshots and replicas.

others.A: Self-managed databases on EC2 keep the full operational burden of patching, backups and HA.
others.C: Amazon S3 is object storage, not a transactional database, and Macie only discovers sensitive data rather than securing a database.
others.D: CloudWatch Logs is for monitoring and logging; it does not protect or encrypt the data.

why: AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes TCP and UDP traffic from the nearest edge location over the AWS global backbone to the closest healthy NLB endpoint. This lowers latency and jitter for multiplayer gaming and supports both protocols on the configured listener ports.

others.A: CloudFront is an HTTP(S) caching CDN and does not accelerate generic UDP game traffic; caching does not apply to live game sessions.
others.B: ALBs only handle HTTP/HTTPS (layer 7) and cannot carry UDP traffic.
others.D: API Gateway handles HTTP/REST/WebSocket APIs, not raw TCP/UDP game traffic, and API caching does not help real-time play.

tip: Non-HTTP (UDP/TCP) global acceleration or static IPs = Global Accelerator; HTTP caching = CloudFront.

why: A Lambda function URL is a built-in dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a function that can be created in one step, with optional IAM or no auth plus CORS settings. The third party can POST the webhook directly to it, so no extra services need to be deployed or managed.

others.B: An ALB works but adds cost and infrastructure to manage for a single function endpoint.
others.C: SNS topics do not expose a public hostname that accepts arbitrary webhook HTTP calls; publishing requires signed AWS API requests.
others.D: SQS queues require authenticated AWS API calls and do not provide a simple public webhook URL.

tip: Simplest public HTTPS endpoint for one Lambda = function URL.

why: Registering the domain and creating a wildcard record (for example *.example.com) in a Route 53 hosted zone gives every customer its own subdomain without per-customer DNS work (A). A wildcard ACM certificate requested in the same Region as a Regional API (D) secures all subdomains, and an API Gateway custom domain name using that ACM certificate (F) maps the subdomains to the REST API.

others.B: For a Regional API endpoint the ACM certificate must be in the same Region as the API (only edge-optimized endpoints use us-east-1).
others.C: Creating a hosted zone per customer is unnecessary operational overhead when a wildcard record covers all customers.
others.E: Creating separate API endpoints for each customer multiplies management effort and is not needed for individual URLs.

tip: Per-customer subdomains: wildcard DNS record + wildcard ACM cert + API Gateway custom domain.

why: Amazon Macie uses managed data identifiers to automatically discover PII in S3 objects and publishes sensitive data findings to Amazon EventBridge. An EventBridge rule matching the SensitiveData finding types can target an SNS topic to email or notify the security team.

others.B: GuardDuty detects threats and anomalous activity, not PII content in S3 objects.
others.C: Macie is correct, but SQS is a queue for application consumers, not a notification mechanism for people.
others.D: GuardDuty does not detect PII, and SQS does not notify humans.

tip: PII in S3 = Macie; notifying people = SNS.

why: Logs stay in S3 Standard for the first 30 days of frequent analysis, then a lifecycle rule transitions them to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for the 60-day backup period, which has a far lower storage price than Standard-IA. An expiration action deletes the objects at 90 days, matching the retention rules most cost-effectively.

others.A: Objects are already in S3 Standard, so this transition does nothing and keeps paying Standard prices during the backup period.
others.B: Moving to Glacier at day 90 while also expiring at day 90 is contradictory, and Standard-IA costs more than Glacier for rarely accessed backups.
others.D: One Zone-IA reduces availability, the day-90 Glacier transition is pointless with deletion at 90 days, and it costs more than Glacier for backups.

tip: Glacier Flexible Retrieval has a 90-day minimum storage charge, but it can still be cheaper than IA for short backup windows; check the math.

why: Amazon EKS supports envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets by associating a customer managed AWS KMS key with the cluster. Once enabled, secrets are encrypted with a data key protected by the KMS key before they are stored in etcd, which meets the requirement directly.

others.A: Secrets Manager stores secrets outside the cluster but does not encrypt the Kubernetes secrets that are stored in etcd.
others.C: The EBS CSI driver provisions persistent volumes for pods and has nothing to do with etcd secret encryption.
others.D: EBS default encryption protects EBS volumes; etcd for EKS runs in the AWS-managed control plane and secret envelope encryption is a separate setting. The aws/ebs alias is reserved for the AWS managed key.

tip: EKS etcd secret encryption = enable KMS envelope encryption on the cluster.

why: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment for PostgreSQL has a writer and two readable standby instances in three AZs, providing high availability with fast failover. The standbys serve read traffic through the reader endpoint with low replication lag, so data scientists get near real-time read-only access without extra read replicas, making it the most cost-effective HA option.

others.A: Scaling up the production instance does not isolate analytic queries from production and stays Single-AZ, so it is not highly available.
others.B: In a Multi-AZ instance deployment the standby cannot serve reads, so data scientists could not use it.
others.C: Multi-AZ instance plus two read replicas means paying for four instances (primary, standby and two replicas), which costs more than a Multi-AZ cluster.

tip: Multi-AZ instance standby = not readable; Multi-AZ DB cluster = two readable standbys.

why: Moving MySQL to an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster gives managed HA across three AZs with readable standbys, ElastiCache for Redis with replication stores session state off the web servers and caches reads, and an Auto Scaling group across three AZs lets the stateless web tier scale with sudden traffic. Every tier becomes both scalable and highly available.

others.B: Only the web tier would scale; session state on the instances and the single EC2 MySQL database remain single points of failure.
others.C: Migrating a relational MySQL application to DynamoDB requires a major rewrite, and the web tier would still not scale across AZs.
others.D: A Single-AZ RDS database does not provide high availability across three Availability Zones.

tip: Make web tiers stateless by moving sessions to ElastiCache or DynamoDB, then scale with Auto Scaling groups.

why: CloudFront geographic restrictions with an allow list let you serve content only to viewers in specified countries, blocking everyone else with an HTTP 403, and you can configure a custom error page. As the rollout expands, you simply add countries to the allow list.

others.B: Signed URLs and cookies control access per user, not by viewer country.
others.C: Encryption protects data but does not restrict viewing by geography.
others.D: Time-restricted signed URLs limit access by time, not location.

tip: Restrict content by country at the CDN = CloudFront geo restriction (allow or block list).

why: The keyed answer uses a warm standby Amazon RDS for SQL Server database kept in sync by AWS DMS with change data capture, so ongoing changes replicate continuously, meeting an RPO of around 30 seconds. A running RDS standby can be promoted and the application redirected well within the 60-minute RTO, without needing SQL Server Enterprise licensing.

others.A: Multi-site active/active with SQL Server Enterprise Always On is the most expensive option and exceeds the RTO need.
others.C: The key treats Elastic Disaster Recovery as not chosen here, although it does offer second-level RPO and minutes-level RTO at low cost.
others.D: Nightly backups give an RPO of up to 24 hours, far beyond 30 seconds.

tip: DR patterns by cost: backup/restore < pilot light < warm standby < multi-site active/active.
flag: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (C) supports SQL Server Standard on VMs with sub-second-to-seconds RPO, minutes RTO and low-cost staging, so it likely meets the needs more cheaply than a running RDS warm standby with DMS; C is arguably correct.

why: Amazon Aurora provides storage replicated six ways across three AZs, fast failover and up to 15 low-latency Aurora Replicas, which improves availability and performance. Reporting can be pointed at the reader endpoint to offload the primary, and Aurora is fully managed, making it the most operationally efficient choice despite the Oracle-to-Aurora migration.

others.A: Using DMS to build instances in multiple Regions is complex and is not how you create a highly available deployment.
others.B: Single-AZ with a read replica in the same AZ is not highly available.
others.C: RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments support only MySQL and PostgreSQL, not Oracle.

tip: RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (readable standbys) = MySQL and PostgreSQL only.

why: For idle, unpredictable traffic, a serverless stack is most cost-effective: Lambda (behind API Gateway) reading user data from DynamoDB costs nothing when idle (A), an Amazon Cognito user pool handles sign-up and sign-in for paying customers (C), and AWS Amplify Hosting serves the static frontend through an integrated CloudFront CDN (E).

others.B: An ECS service behind an ALB with RDS has always-on costs even when the application is idle.
others.D: Cognito identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials (authorization); user authentication is done by user pools.
others.F: S3 static website hosting cannot run server-side code such as PHP.

tip: User pool = authentication (sign-in); identity pool = AWS credentials for authenticated or guest users.

why: CloudFront signed URLs restrict access to individual files, which suits on-demand delivery such as a specific movie rental or music download, and can include expiration times and IP restrictions. Only premium customers receive the signed URLs, so others cannot access the content.

others.A: S3 does not have signed cookies; signed cookies are a CloudFront feature and are best for granting access to many files, not individual purchases.
others.C: Origin access control restricts S3 access to CloudFront but cannot distinguish premium from non-premium viewers.
others.D: Field-level encryption protects specific POST form fields and does not control who can view content.

tip: CloudFront signed URL = individual files; signed cookies = multiple files or whole sections.

why: Savings Plans discounts can be shared only across accounts in the same AWS Organizations consolidated billing family. Creating an organization with a new payer (management) account and inviting the other accounts brings them under consolidated billing (D), and turning on discount sharing in the management account's billing preferences lets the Savings Plan apply across member accounts (A).

others.B: Discount sharing is controlled from the management account of the organization, not from an individual member account.
others.C: Savings Plans cannot be shared through AWS Resource Access Manager.
others.E: This could work technically, but AWS best practice is a dedicated management (payer) account that does not run workloads.

tip: Reserved Instance and Savings Plans sharing works through Organizations consolidated billing, toggled in the management account.

why: API Gateway canary release deployments let you send a configurable percentage of stage traffic to the new API version while the rest continues on the current version, with separate metrics and logs. After verifying the canary, you promote it to production, so customer impact and data loss are minimal and the existing custom domain and Route 53 alias stay unchanged.

others.B: Import in merge mode deploys directly to production for all users at once, with no gradual verification.
others.C: Overwrite mode replaces the whole API definition for all customers at once, risking breakage.
others.D: Creating a new API and switching the alias record cuts over all traffic at once and DNS caching causes inconsistent behavior.

tip: Gradual API rollout in API Gateway = canary release on a stage.

why: The keyed option (its text is missing in this bank) corresponds to a Route 53 active-passive failover configuration: the ALB record is primary with a health check, and a static error page hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket is the secondary. When the health check marks the ALB unhealthy, Route 53 returns the S3 endpoint, which needs minimal changes and no servers.

others.A: Latency routing sends users to the lowest-latency endpoint even when the site is healthy, so some users would see the error page.
others.C: An EC2 instance for the error page adds infrastructure to manage, and the description is really failover, not active-active.
others.D: Multivalue answer routing returns several healthy records at random and is not designed for primary/secondary failover to an error page.

tip: Backup site only when primary is down = Route 53 failover routing with health checks, secondary in S3.

why: AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway presents an iSCSI virtual tape library (VTL) that existing backup applications already understand, so workflows are preserved. Virtual tapes are stored in Amazon S3 and can be archived to S3 Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive, eliminating physical tapes and reducing cost.

others.A: The NFS interface is S3 File Gateway, which would require changing tape-based backup workflows to file-based ones.
others.B: Amazon EFS is file storage and would require changing backup application targets and workflows; it is also costlier than tape archives.
others.C: Amazon EFS does not offer an iSCSI interface.

tip: Replace physical tapes but keep backup software = Tape Gateway (iSCSI VTL).

why: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose (now Amazon Data Firehose) is a fully managed service that ingests high-volume streaming data, scales automatically, buffers and optionally transforms it, and delivers it to Amazon S3 in near real time. No code or servers to manage gives the least operational overhead.

others.B: AWS Glue streaming ETL jobs need to be written, run and paid for continuously and are more effort than Firehose for simple delivery.
others.C: Lambda alone is not an ingestion endpoint for sensor streams and requires custom code to batch and write data.
others.D: AWS DMS migrates and replicates databases; it is not for sensor streaming ingestion.

tip: Stream to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch with no code = Firehose.

why: Grouping the department accounts into OUs in AWS Organizations and attaching service control policies lets you centrally set the maximum services each account can use, applying to every principal in those accounts. It is policy-only and centrally managed, so it has the least operational overhead.

others.A: Systems Manager documents automate operations; they cannot restrict which AWS services accounts use.
others.C: CloudFormation provisions resources but does not prevent users from using other services directly.
others.D: Service Catalog curates approved products but does not block access to other services unless combined with restrictive IAM in every account.

tip: Restrict services per account centrally = SCPs on OUs.

why: A NAT gateway in a public subnet, with the private subnet route table pointing 0.0.0.0/0 to it, lets the database instances initiate outbound connections to the third-party provider while blocking unsolicited inbound connections. It is a managed, highly available service within an AZ, so it maximizes security without adding operational overhead.

others.A: A NAT instance works but must be patched, scaled and made highly available yourself, increasing operational overhead.
others.C: A virtual private gateway connects to VPN or Direct Connect networks, not the public internet, so routing internet traffic there does not reach the provider.
others.D: A virtual private gateway is for private connectivity to on-premises networks and gives no internet access.

tip: Outbound-only internet from private subnets = NAT gateway in a public subnet.

why: For a customer managed KMS key, Lambda decrypts environment variables using the function's execution role, so the execution role needs kms:Decrypt permission in its IAM policy (B). The KMS key policy must also allow that execution role to use the key (D), because key policies are the primary control for KMS key access.

others.A: A Lambda resource-based policy controls who can invoke or manage the function, not what the function can access.
others.C: The function policy is the same as the resource policy and governs invocation, not KMS access.
others.E: Key policies grant access to principals such as roles, not to a Lambda resource policy.

tip: Function's outbound permissions = execution role; who can invoke = resource policy.

why: S3 Standard serves the frequent access in the first week, then a lifecycle rule moves reports to S3 Glacier (Flexible Retrieval), whose standard retrievals complete in about 3-5 hours, meeting the 6-hour requirement at a much lower storage cost than IA for multi-year retention.

others.B: Standard-IA has millisecond access but costs several times more than Glacier for years of storage when retrieval within 6 hours is acceptable; small objects also incur a 128 KB minimum charge.
others.C: Intelligent-Tiering is configured by access tiers, not lifecycle rules to Standard-IA, and has per-object monitoring fees; objects under 128 KB are not auto-tiered.
others.D: Glacier Deep Archive standard retrieval takes up to 12 hours, exceeding the 6-hour limit.

tip: Retrieval within hours: Glacier Flexible (3-5 h standard); Deep Archive is up to 12 h (48 h bulk).

why: A Compute Savings Plan applies automatically to any EC2 instance family, size, Region, OS or tenancy (plus Fargate and Lambda), so changing instance type and family every few months keeps the discount. A 1-year No Upfront term reduces cost without a large upfront payment or long commitment.

others.A: Standard Reserved Instances are tied to an instance family; a 3-year term is a long commitment that does not match frequent family changes.
others.C: Standard Reserved Instances lock in an instance family and Region, so changing families loses the discount.
others.D: EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to one instance family in a Region, so changing family breaks coverage.

tip: Changing instance family/Region/compute service = Compute Savings Plan.

why: Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover PII in S3. Macie is a Regional service, so enabling it in us-east-1 and us-west-2 and creating sensitive data discovery jobs (or automated discovery) analyzes the buckets with minimal setup.

others.B: Security Hub aggregates findings and AWS Config evaluates resource configuration; neither inspects object contents for PII.
others.C: Amazon Inspector scans EC2, ECR images and Lambda for vulnerabilities, not S3 data for PII.
others.D: GuardDuty detects threats and suspicious activity, not PII in objects.

tip: PII discovery in S3 = Macie (enable per Region).

why: Performance data shows high memory utilization for both the SAP application and the SQL Server database, so memory optimized instances (such as R or X families, which include SAP-certified sizes) fit both tiers. Matching instance family to the observed bottleneck is the deciding factor.

others.A: Compute optimized instances have a low memory-to-vCPU ratio, which does not suit the memory-heavy application tier.
others.B: Storage optimized instances target high local disk I/O, not memory demand.
others.D: HPC instances are designed for tightly coupled compute workloads, not a memory-heavy SAP application tier.

tip: Match the bottleneck: memory = R/X, CPU = C, local I/O = I/D, HPC = Hpc.

why: An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for SQS places ENIs in the private subnets, so instances reach SQS privately without traversing the internet. The security group on the endpoint must allow inbound HTTPS from the EC2 instances, giving a secure, tightly scoped connection.

others.B: Placing the endpoint in public subnets is unnecessary; the endpoint should be in the subnets where the instances run, and an endpoint policy alone does not cover network access.
others.C: An SQS access policy is attached to the queue, not to the VPC endpoint, and the public subnet placement is unnecessary.
others.D: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, and a NAT gateway would route traffic over the internet.

tip: Gateway endpoints: only S3 and DynamoDB; everything else uses interface endpoints.

why: An IAM role with the needed DynamoDB read and write permissions, attached to the instances through an instance profile, gives the application temporary credentials automatically from the instance metadata service. No access keys appear in the template, user data or code.

others.A: A role that only reads DynamoDB is insufficient because the application must store as well as retrieve data.
others.C: Passing long-term access keys as parameters exposes credentials and requires rotation.
others.D: Creating an IAM user and passing its keys through user data embeds long-term secrets on instances, which is insecure.

tip: EC2 access to AWS services = IAM role via instance profile, never access keys.

why: Amazon EMR runs distributed frameworks such as Apache Spark that process large semistructured S3 datasets in parallel. EMR Spark can also read from Amazon Redshift (for example with the Spark Redshift connector) to join and enrich the S3 data in the same job.

others.A: Athena is interactive SQL querying rather than a parallel processing framework for heavy transformations, and splitting work between Athena and Glue is more complex.
others.C: Kinesis Data Streams is for real-time streaming ingestion, not for moving existing S3 data into Redshift.
others.D: Lake Formation manages data lake permissions and governance; it does not enrich data with Redshift information.

tip: Big data parallel processing with Spark/Hadoop = EMR.

why: VPC peering connects two VPCs privately over the AWS network with no hourly charge and no per-GB processing fee; within the same AZ traffic is free and across AZs standard inter-AZ data transfer applies. For two VPCs in one Region it is the cheapest option.

others.A: Transit Gateway charges per attachment hour and per GB processed, which is unnecessary for only two VPCs.
others.B: Site-to-Site VPN is meant for on-premises connectivity and adds hourly charges and throughput limits.
others.D: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS; it is costly and not used to link two VPCs.

tip: Two VPCs, simple and cheap = VPC peering; many VPCs = Transit Gateway.

why: The teams applied their own tags, which are user-defined tags; to use them in billing reports and Cost Explorer you select them in the Billing console (B). Cost allocation tags are activated from the Organizations management account (payer account) for consolidated billing (E), after which costs can be grouped by product line.

others.A: AWS-generated tags such as aws:createdBy do not represent the teams' product line tags.
others.C: Resource Groups organize resources but do not activate tags for cost allocation.
others.D: In consolidated billing, only the management account can activate cost allocation tags, not each member account.

tip: Cost allocation tags must be activated in the payer (management) account.

why: AWS Control Tower continuously detects landing zone drift, including changes to the OU hierarchy such as moving, creating or deleting OUs or accounts outside Control Tower, and publishes drift notifications to an SNS topic in the audit account. Subscribing the operations team to that topic gives built-in detection and notification with the least overhead.

others.B: AWS Config rules evaluate resource configurations, and there is no managed Config rule for Organizations OU hierarchy changes.
others.C: A CloudTrail organization trail records the API calls but you would still have to build filtering and alerting yourself.
others.D: CloudFormation drift detection only covers resources managed by the stack and does not track OU structure changes.

tip: OU/landing zone change detection with notifications = Control Tower drift.

why: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache that cuts read latency from milliseconds to microseconds. It is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so the application needs minimal code changes and no cache-population logic, giving the least operational overhead.

others.B: ElastiCache for Redis works but requires the application to implement caching logic such as cache-aside and invalidation.
others.C: ElastiCache for Memcached also requires custom caching code and lacks DynamoDB API compatibility.
others.D: Streams plus Lambda to populate ElastiCache is a custom pipeline with more components to build and operate.

tip: Cache for DynamoDB with minimal code change = DAX.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB (B) keeps traffic on the AWS network, and it works by adding a route with the DynamoDB prefix list targeting the endpoint in the subnet route tables (A). Together these ensure API calls from instances never traverse the internet.

others.C: An interface endpoint for Amazon EC2 provides private access to the EC2 API, not to DynamoDB.
others.D: Gateway endpoints do not use elastic network interfaces; ENIs are used by interface endpoints.
others.E: Gateway endpoints do not have security groups; access is controlled with route tables and endpoint policies.

tip: Gateway endpoint = route table entry, no ENI or security group; interface endpoint = ENI plus security group.

why: Amazon EKS Connector lets you register any conformant Kubernetes cluster, including on-premises clusters, with Amazon EKS so you can view clusters and their workloads in the EKS console alongside EKS clusters. It only needs an agent deployed on each cluster, giving a central view with the least overhead.

others.A: Container Insights collects metrics and logs, but it is a monitoring tool and does not give a unified cluster and workload inventory view of external clusters.
others.C: Systems Manager manages nodes and does not provide a Kubernetes cluster and workload view.
others.D: EKS Anywhere is for running EKS-managed clusters on premises; it is not a central viewer for other clusters and would need cluster rebuilds.

tip: View on-premises or other Kubernetes clusters in the EKS console = EKS Connector.

why: Amazon RDS for MySQL supports transactional purchase workloads, and encrypting the sensitive fields client-side with AWS KMS (for example via the AWS Encryption SDK) before writing them means the database only stores ciphertext. Database administrators can query the tables but cannot read the plaintext without KMS key permissions.

others.A: EBS encryption is transparent to anyone with access to the instance, so administrators could still read the data, and a raw volume is not a transactional database.
others.C: S3 server-side encryption decrypts automatically for authorized users, and S3 is not a transactional database for purchases.
others.D: FSx for Windows file shares are not a transactional database and file permissions do not protect data from administrators.

tip: Protect data even from DBAs = client-side (application-level) encryption.

why: Amazon Aurora MySQL is wire-compatible with MySQL so applications keep working, and AWS DMS can migrate the database with minimal downtime. Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes Aurora Replicas based on load, and Aurora storage grows automatically, so the database scales with demand.

others.A: RDS storage autoscaling only grows disk space; it does not scale compute to handle increased demand.
others.B: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse, not a transactional MySQL-compatible database.
others.D: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database and is not compatible with applications built for MySQL.

why: Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system with a hierarchical directory structure that many Linux instances across multiple AZs can mount concurrently with read-after-write consistency. It scales throughput and capacity automatically for rapid concurrent reads and writes.

others.A: Amazon S3 is object storage with a flat namespace, not a POSIX file system for concurrent file-level writes.
others.C: EBS Multi-Attach works only within a single AZ, requires a cluster-aware file system and supports limited instances.
others.D: Synchronizing separate EBS volumes is custom, error-prone and not truly shared storage.

tip: Shared POSIX file system across AZs for Linux = EFS; Windows = FSx for Windows.

why: API Gateway receives the sensor HTTP requests, Lambda processes and aggregates usage, and DynamoDB stores per-tenant totals with atomic counters, all fully managed and serverless. Each piece is decoupled, so independent components can be added later with the least operational overhead.

others.B: An ELB with an EC2 Auto Scaling group requires managing instances, and S3 is not suited to incrementally adding up usage values.
others.C: SQL Server Express on a self-managed EC2 instance is not a managed database and adds patching and backup overhead.
others.D: EC2 instances plus EFS require server management and a file system is a poor fit for summing per-tenant usage.

tip: Managed HTTP ingestion = API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB.

why: Amazon S3 stores virtually unlimited data (petabytes) durably and cheaply, and Amazon CloudFront caches the drawings at edge locations close to users. This combination minimizes load times while scaling storage without limits.

others.B: S3 Glacier is archive storage with retrieval delays of minutes to hours, unsuitable for viewing drawings on demand.
others.C: EBS volumes are limited in size per volume and attached to single instances, so they do not scale to petabytes for a web application.
others.D: Storage Gateway is for hybrid on-premises access to AWS storage, which is not needed when everything runs on AWS.

why: EventBridge publishes rule metrics to CloudWatch in the AWS/Events namespace, including MatchedEvents (rule conditions met), Invocations (target invoked) and FailedInvocations. Checking these shows whether the rule matches and whether delivery to the API destination is attempted or failing.

others.B: A dead-letter queue only exists if one was configured and only shows failed deliveries, not whether the rule matched.
others.C: EventBridge does not write rule matches to CloudWatch Logs by default unless you add a log group as a target.
others.D: CloudTrail records API calls such as PutRule, not each event match or target invocation.

tip: Is my EventBridge rule firing? Check MatchedEvents and Invocations metrics in AWS/Events.

why: An Auto Scaling group with a scheduled action can raise the desired and maximum capacity to six instances every Friday evening and lower it back to two afterward, using a recurring cron schedule. This fits a predictable, recurring load pattern with no manual work.

others.A: An EventBridge reminder would still require a person or extra automation to change capacity.
others.C: Manual scaling requires someone to change capacity every week.
others.D: Dynamic scaling reacts to metrics after load rises, while the known weekly schedule is handled more simply and proactively by scheduled scaling.

tip: Predictable recurring load = scheduled scaling.

why: ACM cannot issue certificates signed by an external public CA, so the certificate must be obtained from the third-party CA and imported into ACM. An API Gateway custom domain name can then use the imported ACM certificate with a security policy that supports TLS 1.3 to serve the API endpoint.

others.B: ACM only issues certificates from Amazon's own CA (or AWS Private CA), not from a specific third-party public CA.
others.C: ACM cannot create third-party-signed certificates, and Lambda function URLs do not support custom certificates or custom domains.
others.D: ACM cannot issue a third-party-signed certificate, and function URLs cannot use your own certificate.

tip: Third-party CA certificate = import into ACM; ACM-issued certs are always Amazon-signed.

why: Aurora Serverless v2 is MySQL-compatible, fully managed and scales capacity automatically in fine-grained ACU increments as demand changes. Each ACU provides about 2 GiB of memory, so a minimum of 1 ACU covers the 2 GiB baseline while scaling up handles unexpected spikes with the least administration.

others.A: DynamoDB is not MySQL compatible and would require rewriting the application.
others.B: Provisioned Aurora uses instance classes and does not use ACUs or scale compute automatically.
others.D: A fixed RDS for MySQL instance with 2 GiB does not scale compute automatically for unexpected load.

tip: 1 ACU = about 2 GiB memory; variable load on relational DB = Aurora Serverless v2.

why: Lambda SnapStart for Java initializes the function once, snapshots the memory and disk state, and resumes new execution environments from the cached snapshot, reducing startup latency by up to 10 times. It has no extra charge for Java runtimes, making it the most cost-effective way to cut cold starts when strict latency is not required.

others.A: Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts but charges for pre-initialized environments continuously, which is more expensive.
others.B: Increasing the timeout lets functions run longer but does not reduce cold start latency.
others.C: More memory adds CPU and may speed initialization slightly but raises cost and does not address cold starts as effectively.

tip: Java cold starts, cost-sensitive = SnapStart; strict latency = provisioned concurrency.

why: Aurora Serverless v2 for MySQL scales capacity automatically and can scale down to a low minimum (and now auto-pause at 0 ACUs) when idle, so you pay mainly for the 2 hours of weekly use plus storage. That makes it the most cost-effective managed option for such an intermittent workload.

others.B: A provisioned Aurora cluster bills for instances around the clock even when the application is unused.
others.C: A reserved EC2 instance is paid for all week and adds database management overhead.
others.D: Running MySQL on ECS adds container and storage management and is not a managed database.

tip: Intermittent or idle-heavy relational workload = Aurora Serverless v2.

why: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment for PostgreSQL has one writer and two readable standbys in three AZs, giving high availability with fast failover and extra read capacity through the reader endpoint. It delivers both needs in one managed configuration, which is the most operationally efficient.

others.A: DynamoDB is not PostgreSQL, so the application would require a rewrite.
others.B: A Multi-AZ instance deployment has a standby that cannot serve reads, so read capacity does not increase.
others.D: Cross-Region read replicas add read capacity but add cross-Region cost and complexity and do not give automatic HA failover.

tip: HA plus readable standbys in one setting = Multi-AZ DB cluster.

why: An edge-optimized API Gateway endpoint routes requests through the CloudFront edge network to the API's Region, so geographically distributed clients connect to a nearby edge location and get lower latency. This is the endpoint type designed for globally distributed users.

others.A: Private endpoints are reachable only from within a VPC through an interface endpoint, not by public users.
others.B: Regional endpoints suit clients in the same Region; distant users would connect directly to that Region with higher latency.
others.C: An interface VPC endpoint provides private access from a VPC and does nothing for internet users.

tip: Global clients = edge-optimized; same-Region clients = Regional; VPC-only = private.

why: AWS Certificate Manager issues free public TLS certificates that integrate with CloudFront (the certificate must be in us-east-1). With DNS validation, ACM renews the certificate automatically as long as the CNAME validation record remains, so creation and renewal are fully automated.

others.A: A CloudFront security policy selects allowed TLS protocol versions and ciphers; it does not create certificates.
others.B: Origin access control secures CloudFront access to S3 origins and has nothing to do with certificates.
others.D: Email validation requires someone to respond to emails for issuance and renewal, so it is not fully automated.

tip: Automatic ACM renewal = DNS validation.

why: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a managed, write-through in-memory cache for DynamoDB that reduces read response times from milliseconds to microseconds. Because DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB, the serverless application needs minimal changes, giving the least operational overhead.

others.B: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics, not a low-latency cache for an application database.
others.C: Migrating to RDS is a large redesign and does not provide microsecond caching.
others.D: ElastiCache for Redis could cache data but requires custom caching logic in the application.

tip: Microsecond reads for DynamoDB = DAX.

why: Instance Scheduler on AWS is an AWS solution that automatically starts and stops RDS and EC2 instances on defined schedules, such as weekday business hours. Stopping the database outside those hours means paying only for storage during idle time, with no custom code to maintain.

others.B: Turning off automatic backups reduces data protection and barely affects cost, since compute remains the main expense.
others.C: A custom CPU-based Lambda function adds code to build and maintain and is less reliable than a schedule for known hours.
others.D: Reserved instances lower the hourly rate but you still pay for the instance 24/7 even though it is used only during business hours.

tip: Known on/off hours = schedule start/stop (Instance Scheduler); note stopped RDS restarts automatically after 7 days.

why: Hosting the application on EC2 with an EBS gp3 volume keeps a block-storage, single-instance design comparable to locally attached disks, so the architecture does not change. gp3 provides a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s independent of size, at about 20 percent lower cost per GB than gp2, making it the most cost-effective choice.

others.A: FSx for Lustre is a shared high-performance file system, which changes the architecture and costs more.
others.B: gp2 works but costs more per GB than gp3, and its performance is tied to volume size.
others.C: FSx for OpenZFS is a shared network file system, which changes the storage architecture and adds cost.

tip: gp3 beats gp2 on price and decouples IOPS from size.

why: Setting the Auto Scaling group minimum to four with two On-Demand Instances in each of two Availability Zones ensures that if an entire AZ fails, two instances are still running, satisfying the at-least-two requirement. On-Demand Instances avoid Spot interruptions for a stateful production application.

others.A: With one instance per AZ, an AZ outage leaves only one instance running until replacement, violating the two-instance requirement.
others.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted and a single AZ is not fault tolerant.
others.D: Spot Instances in one AZ can be reclaimed, so losing the On-Demand AZ could leave fewer than two instances.

tip: Fault tolerant = survive the loss of one AZ with the required capacity still running.

why: A geolocation routing policy sends users based on their location: users near us-west-1 go to the nearby on-premises data center and users near eu-central-1 go to the AWS Region. This directs each user to the closest site to minimize load time and works with non-AWS endpoints.

others.B: Simple routing returns the same records to everyone and cannot route based on user location.
others.C: Latency routing uses AWS Region latency data; associating it with us-west-1 for on-premises servers would be an approximation, and this option sets only one Region.
others.D: Weighted routing splits traffic evenly regardless of where users are, increasing load time for many users.

why: At 1 Gbps, 5 PB would take over a year to upload, missing the 6-month deadline. Snowball devices with Tape Gateway let you copy physical tapes to virtual tapes offline, ship them to AWS, and then archive the virtual tapes to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest-cost storage for 10-year compliance retention.

others.A: Transferring 5 PB over a 1 Gbps link with DataSync takes well over a year, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive.
others.B: Writing directly over the network suffers the same bandwidth limit and cannot finish in 6 months.
others.D: An on-premises Tape Gateway still uploads over the 1 Gbps connection, which is too slow for 5 PB.

tip: Estimate transfer time: 1 Gbps is roughly 10 TB per day at best; petabytes means Snow Family.

why: A spread placement group places each instance on distinct underlying hardware with separate racks, power and network, and partition placement groups extend this to groups of nodes on separate partitions. This lets you configure the placement so instances do not share the same hardware, reducing correlated failures.

others.B: Separate accounts do not control physical hardware placement.
others.C: Dedicated tenancy isolates your instances from other customers but your own instances can still share the same host hardware.
others.D: Shared tenancy gives no control over hardware placement.

tip: Spread = max 7 instances per AZ on distinct hardware; partition = groups of instances on separate racks for large distributed workloads.

why: On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve EC2 capacity for a specific instance type in a specific Availability Zone for any duration, guaranteeing that the capacity will be available when failover happens. This is the only option that explicitly guarantees capacity in the DR Region.

others.A: On-Demand Instances have no capacity guarantee and may hit insufficient capacity errors during a regional event.
others.B: Savings Plans are a pricing commitment and do not reserve capacity.
others.C: Regional Reserved Instances provide a discount but do not reserve capacity; only zonal RIs reserve capacity.

tip: Guaranteed capacity = Capacity Reservation (or zonal RI); Savings Plans and regional RIs are just discounts.

why: An AWS account can belong to only one organization at a time. The R&D account must first leave the prior organization (which requires it to have standalone billing information), and then the new management account invites it to join the new organization.

others.A: An account cannot be a member of two organizations at the same time.
others.C: Creating a new account and migrating resources is unnecessary effort when the existing account can move.
others.D: A management account cannot be a member of another organization, and an account cannot be in two organizations.

tip: Moving accounts between organizations: leave the old one, then accept the invitation to the new one.

why: Amazon API Gateway provides a public endpoint that other web applications can integrate with, and a Lambda authorizer performs the authorization step before requests are accepted. API Gateway can proxy directly to Kinesis Data Firehose, which scales automatically with sudden spikes and delivers the data to S3 for analytics.

others.A: A Gateway Load Balancer is for deploying third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls and cannot perform authorization; ECS on EFS adds management.
others.B: Kinesis Data Streams does not store data in S3 by itself, and a separate Lambda function is not an authorization step in the request path.
others.D: A Gateway Load Balancer is not meant for web application ingestion, and the setup requires managing containers and storage.

tip: Custom authorization in front of an API = API Gateway Lambda authorizer (or Cognito authorizer).

why: With an RPO and RTO of 24 hours, copying RDS automated snapshots to another Region daily (RDS supports cross-Region automated backup replication) is enough: in a disaster you restore from the most recent copy. It avoids paying for a continuously running standby, making it the most cost-effective option.

others.A: A cross-Region read replica runs a second Enterprise Edition instance continuously, which is expensive and exceeds the requirement.
others.B: DMS cross-Region replication requires running a replication instance and a target database continuously, adding cost.
others.C: Native backups to S3 with cross-Region replication work but involve more setup and slower restores than snapshot copies.

tip: Long RPO/RTO (hours) = backup and restore; seconds/minutes = replicas or warm standby.

why: Storing session state in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis moves it off the web servers, so an instance failure does not lose sessions. Redis supports replication with Multi-AZ automatic failover and persistence, providing high availability for the session store.

others.A: Memcached has no replication or persistence, so a node failure loses session data.
others.C: Storage Gateway cached volumes are for hybrid on-premises storage, not a session store for EC2 applications.
others.D: RDS can store sessions but has higher latency and is more costly than an in-memory store for session data.

tip: HA session store = ElastiCache for Redis (or DynamoDB); Memcached lacks replication.

why: An RDS read replica is kept in sync asynchronously with the primary, and directing the monthly reporting queries to the replica offloads them from the primary. The daily workload keeps its performance without resizing the primary.

others.B: Restoring a backup each month gives stale data and requires repeated manual effort.
others.C: Exporting to S3 and querying with Athena adds a data pipeline and data may be stale.
others.D: Resizing the instance for a once-a-month peak means paying for extra capacity all month.

tip: Offload reporting from the primary = read replica.

why: The AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an Application Load Balancer from Kubernetes Ingress resources, and the ALB does path-based and host-based layer 7 routing to the customer and order microservices. One ALB can serve multiple services, making it the most cost-effective way to route requests.

others.A: A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot route by URL path or host to different microservices.
others.C: A Lambda function to forward requests is custom code that adds latency and cost.
others.D: API Gateway in front of EKS still needs a load balancer or VPC link and adds per-request cost.

tip: Path/host routing to Kubernetes services = ALB via AWS Load Balancer Controller Ingress.

why: S3 stores the images cheaply and CloudFront caches them at edge locations so global customers get fast access. CloudFront geographic restrictions block viewers from specific countries, and signed URLs ensure only paying customers can download the copyrighted images, all at low cost.

others.A: A public bucket exposes copyrighted images to anyone and MFA does not apply to anonymous public access; there is no country blocking or global caching.
others.B: Creating an IAM user per customer does not scale, is not meant for end customers, and provides no geo blocking or edge caching.
others.C: EC2 instances and ALBs for storing images are costly, and deploying per country does not actually block users from other countries.

tip: Paid content + country blocking + global speed = S3 + CloudFront signed URLs + geo restriction.

why: A Multi-AZ Redis replication group with cluster mode shards, each containing a primary and replicas in different AZs, provides node-level redundancy and automatic failover to a replica in another AZ. Spreading shards and replicas across AZs protects against both node failures and AZ failures within the Region without losing data or capacity.

others.B: AOF persistence helps recover data after a restart but does not provide Multi-AZ failover, and it is not supported on newer Redis versions in ElastiCache.
others.C: More read replicas in a single replication group helps, but without sharding the loss of capacity affects the whole dataset; the key prefers sharded Multi-AZ groups.
others.D: Auto Scaling adjusts capacity for load and does not provide failover or data protection.

tip: ElastiCache Redis HA = Multi-AZ with automatic failover and replicas in other AZs.

why: EC2 Auto Scaling warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready, and with hibernation the instances' in-memory state (RAM) is saved to EBS. When scaled out, hibernated instances resume with memory already loaded, eliminating the long launch and warm-up time.

others.A: Running more instances with auto scaling does not reduce the time each new instance needs to launch and load memory.
others.B: Spot Instances lower cost but still need the same launch and load time and can be interrupted.
others.D: Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity but do not speed up application initialization.

tip: Slow-to-initialize apps = Auto Scaling warm pools (stopped, running or hibernated).

why: Dynamic scaling (for example target tracking on CPU or request count) adds instances in response to real-time metrics when sudden traffic arrives on unpredictable days and removes them afterward. You pay for extra capacity only when needed, making it the most cost-effective option.

others.A: Manual scaling cannot react quickly to sudden, random spikes.
others.B: Predictive scaling relies on recurring daily or weekly patterns, which do not exist for random traffic.
others.D: Scheduled scaling needs known times, but the spikes happen on random days.

tip: Random spikes = dynamic (target tracking); recurring pattern = predictive or scheduled.

why: Aurora Serverless v2 is PostgreSQL-compatible and scales capacity automatically in fine-grained increments as demand rises, then scales back down after the sales event. You pay only for capacity used, which handles unpredictable spikes cost-effectively and avoids connection issues caused by an undersized server.

others.B: A single PostgreSQL database on EC2 cannot be auto scaled like a stateless tier; Auto Scaling would launch separate, inconsistent databases.
others.C: A larger RDS instance means paying for peak capacity all month while traffic is unpredictable.
others.D: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse and not suitable as a transactional ecommerce database.

tip: Unpredictable relational load, pay for usage = Aurora Serverless v2.

why: The latency at the start of each day comes from Lambda cold starts after the functions sit idle overnight. Using Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions to raise provisioned concurrency just before employees start keeps execution environments pre-initialized, eliminating the cold start latency, and can be lowered after hours to save cost.

others.A: Throttling limits control request rates; they do not reduce cold-start latency.
others.C: Invoking one function from an alarm warms at most a single environment and is a fragile workaround.
others.D: More memory can speed execution somewhat but does not eliminate cold starts.

tip: Predictable daily cold starts = scheduled provisioned concurrency.

why: An S3 File Gateway presents an SMB share on premises that the devices write .csv files to, storing them as objects in S3 (A). An AWS Glue crawler infers the schema and creates a table in the Data Catalog (C), and Amazon Athena lets analysts run SQL on the S3 data paying only per query (F), which is most cost-effective for periodic queries.

others.B: FSx File Gateway caches access to FSx for Windows File Server, which stores files in FSx rather than S3 and costs more for this use case.
others.D: An EMR cluster is costly and operationally heavy for periodic SQL queries.
others.E: A running Redshift cluster costs more than per-query Athena for occasional queries.

tip: SMB/NFS to S3 = S3 File Gateway; ad hoc SQL on S3 = Glue crawler + Athena.

why: Under the Outposts shared responsibility model, the customer must provide resilient power, cooling and network connectivity to the racks (A), physical security and access control for the data center (C), and plan for enough spare capacity (such as additional ECS capacity) to tolerate server failures and maintenance (F).

others.B: AWS manages the Outposts hypervisor, storage systems and AWS services running on the Outpost.
others.D: AWS is responsible for the availability of the Outposts infrastructure inside the racks, including servers, power supplies and networking equipment.
others.E: AWS performs physical maintenance and replacement of Outposts components.

tip: Outposts: customer handles the facility (power, network, security) and capacity planning; AWS handles the rack hardware and software.

why: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4, supports any TCP port, and can handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency. It can be internet-facing with static IPs, matching the hardware appliance's performance for a nonstandard TCP port.

others.B: An ALB works at layer 7 for HTTP/HTTPS only and cannot handle raw TCP traffic.
others.C: CloudFront handles HTTP/HTTPS on standard ports and cannot listen on arbitrary TCP ports.
others.D: API Gateway handles HTTP/REST/WebSocket APIs, not raw TCP on a custom port.

tip: TCP/UDP, extreme performance or static IPs = NLB.

why: Creating an Aurora read replica of the RDS for PostgreSQL instance continuously replicates data into a new Aurora cluster. When replica lag reaches zero, you stop writes briefly and promote the replica to a standalone Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, giving minimal downtime and data loss with very little operational effort.

others.A: Restoring from a snapshot misses all writes made after the snapshot, causing data loss or longer downtime.
others.C: Importing from S3 requires exporting data first and does not keep the target in sync, causing downtime.
others.D: pg_dump and restore requires downtime for consistency and is slow and manual for a critical database.

tip: RDS MySQL/PostgreSQL to Aurora with minimal downtime = Aurora read replica, then promote.

why: AWS Backup centrally automates backup plans for EC2 instances, creating AMIs with EBS snapshots on a schedule with retention rules and optional cross-Region or cross-account copies. Restores can be scripted for many instances with the AWS Backup API or CLI, giving recoverability for hundreds of instances with the least effort.

others.A: Manual snapshots per instance plus custom CloudFormation templates require significant ongoing effort.
others.B: Elastic Beanstalk is an application deployment service, not a DR mechanism for existing EC2 instances.
others.D: Custom Lambda functions for backup and restore must be written and maintained, which is more effort than AWS Backup.

tip: Centralized, policy-based backup across services = AWS Backup.

why: The Step Functions Map state in Distributed mode runs up to 10,000 parallel child workflow executions and can iterate directly over objects in an S3 bucket or items in large S3 files. It is serverless and designed for large-scale parallel processing of S3 datasets, giving the most operational efficiency.

others.A: Inline Map mode supports only up to 40 concurrent iterations and limited state history, so it does not scale to thousands of items.
others.C: AWS Glue suits ETL jobs but is less suited to arbitrary per-item processing of mixed media, logs and IoT data on demand.
others.D: Coordinating several Lambda functions manually requires custom orchestration, error handling and fan-out logic.

tip: Massive parallel processing over S3 objects = Step Functions Distributed Map.

why: 80 percent of 500 Mbps is 400 Mbps, about 4.3 TB per day, so moving 10 PB over the network would take around 6 years. Multiple AWS Snowball devices transfer the data offline and AWS imports it into S3, which is the only way to finish in 6 weeks.

others.A: DataSync still uses the 400 Mbps link, which is far too slow for 10 PB in 6 weeks.
others.B: rsync over the same limited link is too slow and cannot write directly to S3.
others.C: Parallel CLI copies cannot exceed the available bandwidth, so the transfer would still take years.

tip: Calculate days = data / bandwidth; if it exceeds the deadline, use Snow Family.

why: A Storage Gateway volume gateway presents iSCSI volumes, so existing iSCSI clients need minimal changes. In cached volume mode the primary data is stored in S3 while frequently accessed data is cached locally for low latency, reducing the on-premises storage footprint.

others.A: S3 File Gateway provides NFS/SMB file shares, not iSCSI block storage, so it would require infrastructure changes.
others.B: EBS volumes attach only to EC2 instances in AWS and cannot be mounted by on-premises iSCSI servers.
others.C: Stored volumes keep the full dataset on premises with asynchronous backup to AWS, so it does not reduce on-premises storage dependency.

tip: Volume gateway: cached = data in S3, hot cache locally; stored = data locally, snapshots in AWS.

why: S3 Standard handles frequent access for the first 30 days, then a lifecycle rule moves objects to S3 Standard-IA, which keeps millisecond access and multi-AZ eleven-nines durability at a lower storage price. This satisfies immediate availability for any length of time while minimizing cost.

others.A: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires restores taking minutes to hours, so objects are not readily available.
others.C: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which reduces resilience and does not maximize durability against AZ loss.
others.D: Intelligent-Tiering already moves objects between tiers automatically; adding a lifecycle rule to Standard-IA is redundant and Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring fees.

tip: Needs instant access + rarely read = Standard-IA; One Zone-IA only for re-creatable data.

why: Storing 6 MB documents as blobs bloats the RDS database, increasing expensive EBS storage and hurting performance. Moving the documents to Amazon S3, which is highly durable, highly available and much cheaper per GB, and keeping only metadata and S3 keys in the database shrinks the database and improves performance most cost-effectively.

others.A: Magnetic storage is legacy, slower and would further hurt performance.
others.B: A larger instance and Provisioned IOPS storage greatly increase cost while keeping the blobs in the database.
others.D: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so 6 MB documents cannot be stored as items, and the rewrite is significant.

tip: Large binary objects belong in S3 with pointers in the database.

why: Associating an AWS WAF web ACL with the ALB and using an IP set match rule lets you allow only the registered retail IP addresses and block everything else. IP sets can hold up to 10,000 CIDRs each and several can be referenced, so 20,000 addresses fit, and they can be updated without touching the application.

others.B: Firewall Manager centrally manages WAF and security group policies across accounts; it is unnecessary for one ALB and still relies on WAF rules.
others.C: ALBs do not support Lambda authorizers; that is an API Gateway feature.
others.D: Network ACLs are limited to about 20 rules by default (40 maximum), far too few for 20,000 IP addresses.

tip: Large IP allow lists in front of ALB, API Gateway or CloudFront = AWS WAF IP sets.

why: Lake Formation data filters provide column-level, row-level and cell-level security on Data Catalog tables, so users can query tables while sensitive portions are hidden. It is built-in, declarative permission management, which has the least operational overhead.

others.A: An IAM role granting table access gives access to entire tables and cannot hide specific rows or cells.
others.C: A Lambda function that strips data before ingestion removes it for everyone and is custom code to maintain.
others.D: Periodically deleting sensitive data with Lambda is custom, error prone and leaves exposure windows.

tip: Fine-grained access in a data lake = Lake Formation data filters (row, column and cell level).

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 lets the EC2 instances write to S3 over the AWS network without traversing the internet. AWS Direct Connect provides a private dedicated connection between the on-premises data center and the VPC, so the output is consumed without using the public internet.

others.A: An interface endpoint for EC2 covers the EC2 API, not S3, and Site-to-Site VPN traffic travels over the public internet, even though encrypted.
others.C: Transit Gateway does not connect directly to S3 buckets, and the VPN uses the public internet.
others.D: NAT gateways send S3 traffic over the public internet, violating the compliance requirement.

tip: No public internet at all: VPC endpoints inside AWS, Direct Connect to on-premises (VPN still rides the internet).

why: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams ingests and buffers high-volume data in near real time and scales with shards (or on-demand mode), so spikes are absorbed instead of returning 503 errors. Lambda consumes records from the stream and scales processing automatically, decoupling ingestion from compute capacity.

others.B: A usage plan quota throttles the vendor, which rejects data instead of processing it.
others.C: SNS is a pub/sub notification service without durable buffering for stream processing, and the vendor's REST calls would still hit limited EC2 capacity.
others.D: Containerizing on ECS with the EC2 launch type still has a capacity ceiling and does not buffer spikes.

tip: Ingestion spikes overwhelming compute = put a buffer (Kinesis or SQS) in front and decouple.

why: A VPC endpoint for S3 (gateway or interface) gives the private subnet a route to S3 over the AWS network without internet access. The bucket policy can restrict access with the aws:SourceVpce condition so only requests through that endpoint are allowed.

others.A: An internet gateway sends traffic over the public internet, and bucket policies cannot reference an internet gateway.
others.B: A VPN connects networks to the VPC; it does not provide private access from the VPC to S3.
others.C: A NAT gateway routes S3 traffic through the internet path, violating the requirement.

tip: Restrict a bucket to VPC traffic = VPC endpoint plus aws:SourceVpce in the bucket policy.

why: Amazon EKS supports envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets with an AWS KMS key, which can be enabled on new or existing clusters with one setting. Secrets are then encrypted before being stored in etcd, without any application changes, giving the least operational overhead.

others.A: Encrypting in the application requires code changes and key handling in every container.
others.C: A Lambda function for encryption is custom code and does not integrate with Kubernetes secrets.
others.D: Parameter Store would move secrets outside Kubernetes and require application and integration changes.

tip: EKS secrets encryption at rest = KMS envelope encryption setting on the cluster.

why: An Application Load Balancer in front of the application tier's Auto Scaling group distributes traffic from the web servers, and the application servers' security group allows inbound traffic only from the ALB (with the ALB's security group allowing only the web servers' security group). Security group referencing is stateful and adapts automatically as instances scale.

others.A: PrivateLink is for exposing services across VPCs or accounts, and network ACLs cannot reference changing Auto Scaling instances.
others.B: VPC endpoints provide access to AWS or PrivateLink services; they are not placed in front of your own servers inside the same VPC.
others.C: Network ACLs are subnet-level, stateless and IP-based, so they cannot easily restrict access to dynamically scaling web servers.

tip: Tier-to-tier access control = security groups that reference other security groups.

why: CloudWatch Container Insights collects, aggregates and summarizes metrics and logs from EKS clusters, nodes, pods and services (now with enhanced observability), and displays them in curated CloudWatch dashboards. It is purpose-built for containerized microservices, providing the centralized view required.

others.A: Running the plain CloudWatch agent collects raw metrics and logs but does not automatically aggregate and summarize them per cluster, pod and service.
others.B: App Mesh is a service mesh for traffic management and is being discontinued; it is not a centralized metrics and log console.
others.C: CloudTrail data events record AWS API activity, not application metrics and logs.

tip: Container (ECS/EKS) metrics and logs summarized = CloudWatch Container Insights.

why: Amazon GuardDuty continuously monitors CloudTrail management and S3 data events, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs and runtime activity to detect malicious behavior in the account, workloads and S3 access patterns. Its findings integrate with AWS Security Hub, which aggregates and displays them on dashboards.

others.A: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 rather than monitoring for malicious activity, and AWS Config is not a findings dashboard.
others.B: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, and CloudTrail records API calls; it does not display security findings.
others.D: AWS Config evaluates resource configuration compliance, not malicious activity.

tip: Threat detection = GuardDuty; central findings dashboard = Security Hub.

why: Amazon EFS provides a managed NFS file system that many AWS resources can mount concurrently (B). An AWS DataSync agent on premises copies the 200 GB from the NFS server to EFS online, with incremental transfers and verification, so existing services keep running during migration (E).

others.A: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system for HPC workloads and is more expensive than EFS for general NFS use.
others.C: Amazon S3 is object storage and is not accessed natively with NFS by AWS resources.
others.D: Manual OS copy commands lack incremental sync, verification and scheduling, risking interruption and inconsistency.

tip: NFS migration to AWS = DataSync to EFS.

why: A Multi-AZ FSx for Windows File Server deployment keeps a standby file server in another AZ, so planned maintenance and AZ disruptions fail over automatically with minimal data loss. AWS Backup copies backups to us-west-2, and Vault Lock in compliance mode with a 5-year minimum retention prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting them.

others.A: Single-AZ 2 deployments have no standby in another AZ, so maintenance or an AZ disruption causes downtime and potential data loss.
